source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: During training, each token is routed to selected experts in a teacher-forced forward pass; router and expert weights receive gradients, while backward activations, optimizer state, microbatching, and capacity handling affect memory and communication. During inference, weights are fixed: prompt tokens are processed in prefill and generated tokens in decode, commonly with KV-cache reuse, dynamic batching, queueing, and latency constraints. Mechanism: top-k routing creates token-to-expert assignments, followed by dispatch to expert owners, expert computation, and combine; instrument these phases separately. Boundary: training throughput or active FLOPs do not establish serving latency or quality, because decode batch sizes, routing skew, interconnect saturation, and overflow/fallback policy can differ materially.
risks: Training and inference have different memory lifetimes, batching, and communication patterns.
Capacity overflow or fallback can change outputs while affecting apparent performance.
evidence_required: Model, phase, sequence lengths, batch/concurrency, router top-k, capacity/overflow policy, precision, topology, and cache settings.
Separate forward/backward and prefill/decode timings, expert-load and overflow telemetry, memory, latency percentiles, throughput, failures, and quality.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Training routes many teacher-forced tokens through selected experts and updates router, expert, and shared parameters with backpropagation; activation storage, optimizer state, microbatch schedule, and all-to-all traffic are part of its cost. Inference uses fixed weights, processes a prompt in prefill and generated tokens step by step in decode, and may reuse the KV cache; serving adds admission, queueing, and dynamic batching concerns. Mechanism: routing scatters token activations to selected expert ranks and gathers/combines their outputs. Boundary: a training speedup cannot be generalized to inference, especially when decode has small or changing batches, hot experts, limited capacity, or a saturated network.
risks: Comparing tokens per second across phases can conceal different work and quality constraints.
Expert imbalance and overflow may produce tail latency or output changes.
evidence_required: Phase definitions, model and quality target, routing/capacity behavior, batching, precision, hardware topology, and cache policy.
Phase-specific compute/communication/memory measurements, expert histograms, queueing and latency tails, overflow/errors, throughput, and quality.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: In training, routing occurs on teacher-forced sequences and gradients update the router and experts, so backward activations, optimizer states, microbatch scheduling, and distributed synchronization matter. In inference, parameters are fixed; prefill routes the prompt and decode routes each newly generated token, often reusing KV state, with serving batches and queueing changing over time. Mechanism: top-k router assignments require scatter/dispatch to expert owners, expert execution, and gather/combine plus synchronization. Boundary: active-compute reduction is not a universal inference benefit; small decode batches, skewed assignments, capacity overflow, or network bandwidth can dominate and reverse the result.
risks: Training memory and communication cannot be inferred from serving memory or latency.
Overflow, drops, or fallback routing can alter correctness and quality.
evidence_required: Training versus serving phase, lengths, batching, router/capacity settings, topology, precision, and KV-cache policy.
Forward/backward and prefill/decode timing breakdowns, memory high-water marks, expert balance, communication, latency/throughput, overflow, and quality.

source_user: Explain how MoE changes between training and inference. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Training uses teacher forcing and backpropagation through router and expert choices, with activation memory, optimizer state, gradient communication, and microbatch bubbles affecting cost. Inference has frozen weights and separates prompt prefill from autoregressive decode; KV-cache reuse, request arrivals, dynamic batching, queueing, and latency percentiles become central. Mechanism: top-k routing dispatches activations to selected experts, runs expert computation, and combines results, adding communication and synchronization to both phases. Boundary: results from a training batch or prefill benchmark do not predict decode behavior; low concurrency, hot experts, capacity limits, or interconnect saturation can remove MoE gains.
risks: Different batch composition and work per token make cross-phase throughput comparisons misleading.
Cache pressure and overflow policy can affect serving performance and output quality.
evidence_required: Matched model/quality assumptions, phase and length distributions, batch/load policy, routing/capacity settings, topology, precision, and cache configuration.
Repeated phase-specific latency, throughput, memory, communication, expert-load, overflow/error, and quality measurements.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: because only a few experts execute for each token, an MoE model is automatically faster and cheaper than a dense model. Correction: top-k routing reduces selected expert compute, but dispatching activations to expert owners, synchronization, and combining outputs add communication and buffering; all experts may still consume resident memory. Boundary: the claim may fail for small batches, skewed routing, long or dynamic requests, limited interconnect bandwidth, or capacity overflow. Test it only with a quality-matched baseline and measured prefill/decode latency, throughput, memory, errors, and tail percentiles.
risks: Active FLOPs can be mistaken for end-to-end serving cost.
Overflow or fallback can improve nominal throughput while changing outputs.
evidence_required: Matched dense/comparator quality, hardware/topology, precision, routing top-k, capacity policy, workload, and load range.
Expert balance, dispatch/combine time, per-device memory, phase latency, throughput, tail latency, errors, and quality.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: an MoE with fewer active parameters per token necessarily uses less memory. Correction: routing selects top-k experts for computation, but expert weights can remain resident or be sharded/replicated, while KV cache, activations, dispatch buffers, and communication add memory; active compute is not resident memory. Mechanism: token assignments are scattered to expert ranks and outputs are gathered and combined. Boundary: memory and latency depend on placement, batch/sequence lengths, cache size, and capacity policy, so a claim from one topology or load cannot be generalized. Measure per-device high-water marks and phase-specific performance against a matched baseline.
risks: Aggregate memory can hide a device-level out-of-memory bottleneck.
Sharding and replication can change communication and memory without changing the abstract MoE model.
evidence_required: Expert placement, sharding/replication, precision, sequence/batch/load distributions, cache policy, and comparator.
Per-device weights/activation/KV/temporary memory, routing and communication traces, latency, throughput, failures, and quality.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: an MoE is faster simply because its total parameter count is large but only a small subset is active. Correction: the router's top-k assignments trigger token dispatch, expert execution, and result combination; communication, synchronization, load imbalance, and scheduling can dominate the selected expert compute. Boundary: gains measured with balanced, large batches may disappear for skewed production traffic, low concurrency, or saturated links. Establish a matched quality baseline and measure prefill/decode latency percentiles, throughput or goodput, expert utilization, overflow, memory, errors, and variance.
risks: Parameter count and theoretical active FLOPs are not end-to-end performance measurements.
Average results may hide hot experts and p95/p99 regressions.
evidence_required: Matched quality, workload/load sweep, batch policy, topology, precision, routing top-k, and capacity/overflow handling.
Per-expert load, dispatch/combine and synchronization timing, phase latency, throughput, memory, errors, overflow, and repeated trials.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: routing only a few experts makes MoE latency predictable and uniformly low. Correction: the router creates a variable token-to-expert distribution; dispatch/combine and synchronization wait on communication and the slowest or hottest expert, while capacity limits may drop, reroute, or defer tokens. Boundary: a balanced synthetic benchmark does not support claims about skewed traffic, changing arrival rates, or another interconnect. Validate with representative load sweeps, repeated runs, p50/p95/p99 latency, queueing, expert histograms, overflow/errors, throughput, memory, and output quality.
risks: Mean latency can conceal synchronization and hot-expert tail effects.
Overflow handling can create silent quality regressions or non-comparable results.
evidence_required: Traffic and load distribution, topology, batch/admission policy, routing/capacity/fallback settings, and quality-matched comparator.
Per-expert queue/load, communication and synchronization traces, tail latency, throughput, memory, overflow/errors, and quality.

source_user: Give one misleading intuition about MoE and correct it. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Misleading intuition: fewer active experts means an MoE always costs less per request. Correction: top-k routing saves some expert arithmetic but adds activation scatter/gather, synchronization, buffering, and possibly cross-device all-to-all; total resident weights and KV cache still contribute to memory and cost. Boundary: the conclusion is workload- and system-specific and can reverse at low batch size, imbalanced routing, capacity overflow, long-context memory pressure, or network saturation. Report measured cost with a matched quality baseline, explicit units, phase split, latency tails, throughput, memory, failures, and quality.
risks: Compute-only accounting can omit communication, memory, and service-level costs.
Different quality targets or overflow behavior invalidate cost comparisons.
evidence_required: Cost definition, quality target, comparator, precision, hardware/topology, routing/capacity policy, workload, and load range.
Phase-specific timing, communication, memory high-water marks, expert balance, tail latency, throughput/goodput, errors, and quality with uncertainty.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Use a quality-matched MoE and dense comparator with the same tokenizer, precision, hardware, runtime, service limits, and request set. Start with a fixed prompt/output-length set, then sweep concurrency or offered load and at least two batch policies; separate prefill from decode, warm up, randomize trial order, and repeat runs. Mechanism: instrument top-k routing, token dispatch to expert owners, expert execution, gather/combine, and synchronization to identify whether communication offsets compute savings. Record TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput/goodput, peak per-device memory, expert-load imbalance, overflow/reroutes, errors, and quality. Boundary: this small experiment supports only the tested model, topology, workload, and load range; balanced prompts or one batch size cannot justify a production-wide claim.
risks: A small prompt set may not represent routing skew or production tails.
A comparator with different quality or service policy can create a false speedup.
evidence_required: Exact model/comparator, quality evaluation, prompt and output distributions, load sweep, batch/admission policy, precision, topology, and capacity settings.
Repeated phase-aware measurements, expert histograms, communication traces, memory, latency percentiles, throughput, overflow/errors, and quality.
